definition: For a fixed-frequency CPU execution interval with matching counts, execution time is completed instruction count times cycles per instruction times clock period. Off-CPU waiting and varying clocks need separate accounting.
example: 2 × 10⁹ instructions at CPI 1.5 on a 3 GHz clock take exactly 1 second.

definition: The number of architecturally completed instructions in a measured execution interval, not source lines or the static size of a binary. A three-instruction loop repeated a million times contributes three million instructions.
example: Halving IC at the same CPI and clock halves the run time.

definition: Cycles per instruction: total clock cycles divided by instructions completed over a run. An average, not the latency of any one instruction; below 1 on cores that finish several instructions per cycle.
example: 3 × 10⁹ cycles for 2 × 10⁹ instructions is a CPI of 1.5.

definition: Instructions per cycle: instructions completed divided by clock cycles, the reciprocal of CPI. Often quoted for modern cores because they can complete more than one instruction per cycle.
example: perf stat showing 6 billion instructions in 3 billion cycles reports 2.00 IPC (CPI 0.5).

definition: The duration of one clock cycle, the reciprocal of the clock frequency. In a pipeline it must fit the slowest stage plus pipeline-register overhead.
example: A 3 GHz clock has a period of about 0.333 ns; a 200 ps period is a 5 GHz clock.

definition: How many clock cycles a processor runs per second, measured in hertz. Higher is not automatically faster, because cycles per instruction and instruction count also matter.
example: A 3 GHz core ticks 3 × 10⁹ times per second.

definition: One tick of the processor clock: the basic unit of time in which pipeline stages do their work and pipeline registers latch new values.
example: In the five-stage pipeline each instruction spends one clock cycle in each stage.

definition: The time accounted to a program or thread while it executes on a processor, including relevant on-CPU stalls. It differs from elapsed time, which can also include time descheduled or waiting off-CPU.
example: A program can take 4 s of CPU time but 10 s of wall-clock time if it waits on the disk.

definition: Real elapsed time from start to finish, as a clock on the wall would measure it, including any time spent waiting rather than computing.
How many times faster one version is than another: the old (or other) run time divided by the new one. 1.5 means "50% faster", not "50% less time".
example: 0.667 s versus 0.6 s is a speedup of about 1.11.

definition: The proportions of different instruction classes (ALU operations, loads, stores, branches) that a program executes. In a simple model, CPI is the mix-weighted average of each class's cycle cost.
example: A mix of 50% ALU at 1 cycle, 20% loads at 5, 10% stores at 3 and 20% branches at 2 gives CPI 2.2.

definition: MIPS as a performance metric: instructions executed per second, in millions. Misleading across compilers or ISAs, because it ignores how many instructions the task needs.
example: 1.2 × 10⁹ instructions in 1.2 s is 1,000 MIPS.

definition: Floating-point operations per second, a measure of numerical throughput. A peak figure assumes specified operations and utilisation; sustained performance depends on the workload and counting convention.
The mistaken belief that a higher clock frequency alone means a faster processor, ignoring cycles per instruction and instruction count.

The event-counting mode of the Linux perf tool, which can report events such as cycles, completed instructions and branch misses. Available counters, event meanings, permissions and multiplexing affect what a particular run can measure.
example: perf stat -e branches,branch-misses ./prog counts branch mispredictions.

definition: Processor facilities that count selected events, such as cycles, retired instructions or cache events. Exact event definitions and availability are processor-specific; tools such as perf read them for performance analysis.
How a particular processor implements an instruction set: its pipeline, caches, predictors and execution units. Two chips with the same ISA can have very different microarchitectures and CPI.

The fabrication technology used to build semiconductor circuits. Process generations can improve density, energy or speed, but a node name is not a literal measurement of every transistor dimension and does not guarantee uniform gains.

Complex instruction set computer: an ISA design tradition with comparatively complex operations and addressing modes. x86 is an example; variable instruction length and memory operands are characteristics of that ISA, not a definition applying to every CISC design.
example: x86 rep movsb copies a whole block of memory with one instruction.

definition: Reduced instruction set computer: an ISA design tradition favouring regular encodings and register arithmetic with explicit data loads and stores. Compressed encodings, atomics and instruction fetch require qualifications to any claim that all instructions are fixed-length or only loads/stores access memory.
example: RISC-V, MIPS and ARM are RISC instruction sets.

definition: An instruction-set family implemented by processors from Intel and AMD, among others. Conventional x86 instructions have variable length, up to 15 bytes; many high-performance implementations decode them into internal micro-operations.

An open-standard instruction-set architecture with a base integer register x0 that always reads zero. Base instructions are 32 bits; compressed extensions add shorter encodings, so not every RISC-V instruction is four bytes.
example: lw x1, 8(x2) loads the word at address x2 + 8 into x1.

definition: A RISC instruction-set family whose classic implementations helped establish the five-stage pipeline teaching model. Register zero discards writes; delay-slot behaviour depends on the ISA revision and branch form.

AArch64 is Arm’s 64-bit execution state; its A64 instruction set uses fixed-width 32-bit instructions. A64 has no architectural branch delay slots and includes conditional-select instructions such as CSEL.
Arithmetic logic unit: the circuit that performs integer arithmetic and logic operations such as add, subtract, AND and compare. In the five-stage pipeline it works in the EX stage.

A hardware block carrying out operations such as integer arithmetic, multiplication or loads and stores. Which units exist, how many operations they accept, and their result latencies depend on the implementation.

The processor structures that manage data-memory operations, including address generation, load/store queues, ordering checks and cache requests. The division of this work among pipeline stages differs by implementation.
Program counter: architectural state identifying an instruction address. A speculative front end can track several predicted addresses; a predictor can use address bits to index its tables.
example: In the uncompressed RV32I teaching trace, the sequential next instruction is four bytes after the current one.

definition: An implementation’s array of register storage, with ports for reading operands and writing results. Supporting many simultaneous accesses can increase port count, area and power; banking and other organisations trade access patterns against these costs.
The part of a machine instruction that says which operation to perform, such as add or load.
Widening a signed binary number by copying its sign bit into the new high bits, so its value is unchanged. ID sign-extends an instruction's immediate value before EX uses it.
example: The 12-bit two’s-complement bit pattern 0xFFF represents −1; extending it to 32 bits gives 0xFFFFFFFF, still −1.

definition: A small, fast cache holding recently used instructions, read by the fetch stage. Bigger code, for example from loop unrolling, can cause more instruction-cache misses.
A small, fast cache holding recently used data, read and written by loads and stores in the MEM stage.

An access whose required instruction or data is absent from a particular cache level. It must be supplied or handled by another path, potentially another cache or main memory; latency depends on the system and state.
example: A hypothetical 80 ns miss spans 320 cycles at a fixed 4 GHz; this is a teaching assumption, not a universal DRAM latency.

definition: An organisation with separate instruction and data paths or first-level caches while software uses a shared address space. Independent ports can avoid the simple five-stage conflict between instruction fetch and a data-memory access, subject to resource availability.
A circuit that selects one of several inputs to pass to its output, according to a control signal. Forwarding uses multiplexers in front of the ALU inputs.
Logic with no stored state: after propagation delay its outputs are determined by current inputs. The longest relevant propagation path contributes to the pipeline stage’s timing budget.
The difference in arrival time of the same clock edge at different parts of a chip. It must be budgeted in the clock period.

How long a storage element’s input must be stable before its active clock edge to be captured reliably. Together with other register and clock timing, it contributes to a synchronous pipeline’s timing budget.
A transition of a clock signal. An edge-triggered register captures its input on its designated rising or falling edge, subject to timing requirements.

Overlapping computations by dividing them into stages separated by storage. An ideal scalar instruction pipeline can begin one instruction per cycle; hazards, stage timing and resource limits affect achieved throughput and latency.
example: In the unstalled five-stage scalar teaching model, up to five instructions occupy different stages.

definition: One portion of a pipelined computation between storage boundaries. In the five-stage teaching processor the stages are instruction fetch, decode, execute, data memory and write-back; other implementations divide work differently.

Instruction fetch: reading the next instruction from memory (normally through the instruction cache) at the address in the PC. In the five-stage pipeline it is the first stage, which also computes the next sequential PC.
Instruction decode, the second pipeline stage: work out what the instruction is, read its source registers and sign-extend any immediate value.
Execute, the third pipeline stage: the ALU performs the operation or computes a load/store address.
Memory access, the fourth pipeline stage: loads read and stores write the data cache.
Write back, the fifth pipeline stage: the result is written into the destination register.

A register between two pipeline stages that captures, at each clock edge, everything the instruction needs next: operand values, destination register and control signals. Named after the stages it separates.
example: The ID/EX register holds the operands that EX will use next cycle.

definition: A processor that executes each instruction completely in one long clock cycle, which must fit the slowest instruction. Simple, but most of the hardware sits idle.

The partially occupied start and end of a pipeline run. An initially empty, unstalled scalar pipeline completing at write-back takes one cycle per instruction plus one fewer cycle than its number of stages.
How evenly work is divided among pipeline stages. Balanced stages take equal time; unbalanced stages leave faster stages waiting because the clock must fit the slowest stage plus boundary overhead.

An instruction pipeline that accepts at most one instruction per cycle under the stated counting convention. In the ideal steady-state scalar model, this limits throughput to one instruction per cycle; finite runs and stalls raise CPI.

Instructions whose encodings have the same size within the specified set, such as the 32-bit base RV32I instructions. Extensions can introduce other sizes; x86 instead uses variable-length instructions.

An ISA organisation where ordinary data arithmetic uses registers and explicit loads/stores transfer data to memory. Instruction fetch and specialised operations such as atomics lie outside that simplified description; the ISA does not prescribe one memory pipeline stage.

Placing a value at a byte address divisible by its size, such as a four-byte word at an address divisible by four. It avoids a cache-line split when the access size divides, and does not exceed, the line size.

An implementation’s internal operation used to execute decoded instructions. A machine instruction can produce one or several micro-operations, and some implementations fuse work; these counts are not interchangeable with architectural instructions.

A resource, data or control-flow condition that prevents an instruction proceeding in its intended pipeline slot without special handling. It may be handled by waiting, bypasses, prediction or more resources.
A hazard where two instructions need the same piece of hardware, such as a single memory port, in the same cycle.
A hazard where an instruction needs a result an earlier instruction has not produced yet (or the order of register reads and writes could go wrong).
A hazard caused by branches: the processor does not yet know which instruction to fetch next until the branch is resolved.

Delaying progress in some part of a pipeline until a resource, value or control condition permits continuation. Its effect on total CPI depends on overlap and which stages are held; in the simple scalar model a bubble may be inserted while earlier stages wait.
example: With no bypasses and same-cycle write-before-read, a back-to-back dependent add/sub pair waits two cycles in the stated five-stage model.

definition: A do-nothing pipeline slot left by a stall or flush. Hardware can mark it invalid or disable effects; it need not correspond to a fetched NOP instruction.
Read after write: a later instruction reads a register an earlier one writes, so data really flows between them. It cannot be renamed away, only waited for or forwarded.
example: add x1, x2, x3 then sub x4, x1, x5 is a RAW dependence on x1.

definition: Write after read: a later instruction overwrites a register an earlier one still needs to read. A name dependence, removed by register renaming.
Write after write: two instructions write the same register and the final value must be the later one's. A name dependence, removed by register renaming.
An ordering constraint (WAR or WAW) that exists only because two instructions reuse a register name, not because data flows between them.

Supplying an operand from a producer’s available result path before its normal register-file read would obtain the value. The five-stage model bypasses from EX/MEM or MEM/WB into EX; exact paths and remaining stalls depend on the design.
example: With the stated EX bypass, an add followed by an EX-consuming dependent sub needs no stall.

definition: Control selecting an available producer result for a consumer operand. The five-stage example prefers the newest matching register writer, excludes x0, and must stall if that writer is a load whose data is not yet available.

A consumer needs data from an unfinished load before the available bypass can deliver it. In the stated five-stage cache-hit model, a load followed immediately by an EX-consuming dependent operation needs one stall; other consumers and pipelines can differ.
Control that recognises dependencies or resource conflicts requiring a wait. In the five-stage load-use example it holds fetch/decode while inserting an empty execute slot.

Ordering operations to meet dependencies and use available resources efficiently. A compiler can move independent work into a predictable load-use gap only when values and observable memory behaviour remain valid.
A register that always reads as zero and ignores writes, x0 in RISC-V and register 0 in MIPS. Forwarding logic must not forward values "written" to it.
Discarding wrongly fetched or speculatively executed instructions, turning them into bubbles, typically after a mispredicted branch or an exception.
An instruction that can change which instruction runs next. A conditional branch is taken (jumps to its target) or not taken (falls through) depending on a condition.
A branch is taken when it jumps to its target, and not taken when execution falls through to the next instruction.
The address a branch jumps to when it is taken.
Guessing a branch's direction (and target) before it is resolved, so fetch can continue without waiting. Wrong guesses are flushed, costing a misprediction penalty.
A wrong branch prediction. The processor must discard the wrong-path work and refetch from the correct path.
example: At 95% accuracy, 5 in every 100 branches mispredict.

definition: The fraction of evaluated branch predictions that are wrong, one minus accuracy for the same predictions. In an additive nonoverlapping penalty model, branch fraction times miss rate times recovery cycles gives extra CPI.
example: A 95% accurate predictor has a misprediction rate of 5%; with 20% branches and a 15-cycle penalty that adds 0.2 × 0.05 × 15 = 0.15 to CPI.

definition: The additional execution cost associated with a wrong branch prediction, often expressed in cycles for a stated workload and model. Resolution timing, refetch, dependencies and overlapping work affect it; pipeline depth alone does not determine it.
example: In a hypothetical additive model, 15 lost cycles on 1% of instructions adds 0.15 cycles per instruction.

definition: Prediction by a fixed rule that does not learn from history, such as always predicting not taken, or backward taken, forward not taken.
Backward taken, forward not taken: a static rule that predicts backward branches (usually loops) taken and forward branches not taken.

A table holding learned branch-prediction state, such as two-bit counters. A simple bimodal table uses selected branch-address bits, while history-based predictors use additional context; terminology varies between designs.

A predictor state that remembers the last mapped outcome and predicts it again. For a dedicated counter in a repeated loop with multiple taken outcomes followed by one not-taken exit, it misses at the exit and the next entry after warm-up; not every loop has that pattern.
A predictor entry holding 0 to 3: taken counts up, not taken counts down, stopping at the ends, and it predicts taken at 2 or 3. A single surprise from a strong state does not flip its prediction.
Resistance to change: a 2-bit counter in a strong state needs two opposite outcomes before its prediction flips.

Different branches or history contexts map to the same prediction entry. Their updates can interfere destructively, but sharing can also be neutral or helpful; finite capacity and tags do not eliminate every conflict.

A hardware history of recent branch outcomes used as prediction context. The teaching model shifts one Boolean result per observed branch and uses 1 for taken; real predictors also need policies for speculative history and recovery.
A register whose bits move along by one position each time a new bit is shifted in, so it holds the last few bits seen.
A branch predictor (McFarling, 1993) that XORs the global history register with the branch's PC to index a table of 2-bit counters, so the same branch uses different counters in different contexts.
example: PC bits 1011 XOR history 0110 select counter 1101, entry 13.

definition: Exclusive or: a bitwise operation whose result bit is 1 when exactly one of the two input bits is 1. Written ⊕ in formulas and ^ in Python and C.
A branch predictor that runs two or more predictors (such as local and global history) and uses a trained chooser to pick which one to trust for each branch.

TAgged GEometric history length prediction: a base predictor plus tagged tables with geometrically increasing history lengths. The Seznec–Michaud design uses matching history/tag information and prediction-selection policies; it is not a guarantee that a long history always helps.

A branch predictor (Jiménez and Lin, 2001) built from perceptrons: a perceptron is a simple learned model that multiplies each input by a trained weight, adds a bias and predicts from the sign of the sum. Here the inputs are recent branch outcomes; a single perceptron can only learn linearly separable patterns.

A predictor structure associating instruction addresses with candidate branch information and targets. In the early-fetch teaching design it supplies a target before full decoding; real front ends organise target and direction prediction differently.

A finite hardware structure predicting return targets from recognised call/return behaviour. Conceptually calls push return addresses and returns pop them; overflow, unusual control flow and speculative recovery can lose synchronisation.

A predictor for the target of a branch or jump whose target is computed at run time, such as a virtual call or interpreter dispatch. Implementations may use the branch address and history to distinguish targets.

An architecturally defined instruction position after a branch. Classic MIPS normal delay slots execute on either branch outcome; branch-likely forms have annulment rules, and later ISA revisions can differ. RISC-V and A64 have no architectural branch delay slot.

An instruction conditionally selecting or copying a value without a control-flow jump, such as x86 CMOVcc or A64 CSEL. It can help unpredictable conditions, but dependency costs and workload determine performance.
Code written to compute a result without conditional branches, for example with a conditional move or arithmetic on a comparison result. Not always faster: measure.

Compiler branch-probability hints such as GCC/Clang __builtin_expect and C++ likely/unlikely attributes. They can influence code layout and optimisation but do not command a particular hardware predictor outcome.
Compiling a program, running it on typical input to record which paths and branches are hot, then recompiling using that profile.

An interpreter dispatch organisation in which handlers can use distinct indirect branch sites to reach the next operation. Compiler lowering determines whether those sites remain distinct; a central switch can sometimes compile similarly.

A table used to select a code destination from an input value, often in a switch implementation. The compiler chooses whether to use such a table or another lowering, and dispatch details are target-specific.

A family of transient-execution attacks that exploit speculative behaviour and observable side effects. Original variants used conditional-branch or indirect-branch mistraining; applicable mechanisms and mitigations depend on the processor and software.

A transient-execution vulnerability demonstrated on affected processors, allowing protected data to influence observable microarchitectural state before a fault is handled. It does not mean every processor exposes kernel memory or that branch prediction is the required cause.
A processor that can start more than one instruction per cycle, so CPI can fall below 1.

The maximum number of operations a specified issue stage can send to execution per cycle. Fetch, decode, rename, allocation and retirement widths are separate limits, and instruction/micro-operation counting must be stated.

Independent operations in an instruction stream that could overlap if resources permit. True dependencies restrict this parallelism; branches, fetching, scheduling capacity and memory behaviour affect how much a processor can exploit.

Scheduling and executing ready operations beyond an older blocked operation while preserving the architectural contract. Many modern speculative cores retire in order, but out-of-order execution itself does not imply that historical designs all had precise in-order retirement.

Executing or issuing operations in program order under a stated stage convention. In the simple in-order issue model, a blocked instruction prevents younger instructions from issuing past it, even if they are independent.
The part of a core that fetches, decodes and (in out-of-order cores) renames instructions and feeds them to the back end. Guided by the branch predictor.

Giving simultaneously live versions of an architectural register distinct producer identities or storage. This removes register-name WAR and WAW dependencies while preserving RAW data flow; tags and explicit physical registers are different implementations.
A register named by the instruction set, such as x1 to x31 in RISC-V, as opposed to the larger pool of physical registers inside the core.

An implementation storage register used for a value version. A physical-register-file renaming design commonly has more storage than architectural register names, while other renaming designs keep speculative results elsewhere.
The renaming table that maps each architectural register to the physical register holding its newest value.
A list of resources that are currently unused and available to hand out. In register renaming, it holds the physical registers not holding a live value; renaming takes one for each new destination.

The state defined by the ISA, such as architectural registers, instruction position and memory. A speculative core must expose valid committed execution; store visibility can occur after retirement, and speculative microarchitectural effects can still be observable indirectly.
An out-of-order scheduling scheme (Robert Tomasulo, IBM System/360 Model 91, 1967) using reservation stations, producer tags and a common data bus. Tags rename registers implicitly.
A 1960s IBM high-performance mainframe whose floating-point unit introduced Tomasulo's algorithm.
In Tomasulo's algorithm, a buffer in front of a functional unit holding a waiting instruction and, for each operand, either its value (V) or the tag (Q) of the station that will produce it.
In Tomasulo's algorithm, a table recording which reservation station tag will write each register next, blank if the register file value is current.
In Tomasulo's algorithm, the bus that broadcasts each result as a (tag, value) pair to every reservation station and the register file at once.

In Tomasulo's algorithm, the name of the reservation station that will produce a value. A waiting instruction holds the tag instead of the value, and grabs the value when a matching (tag, value) pair is broadcast; this renames registers implicitly.

A structure tracking in-flight operations in program order so completed older work can retire and faults can be handled precisely. Depending on design, values live in ROB entries or in physical registers; the ROB does not force execution order or erase speculative cache effects.

Making an instruction’s completed work architecturally committed. The speculative out-of-order teaching design retires oldest first; a retired store may still wait before other observers see its memory update.

An exception presented as occurring at an exact instruction boundary: older instructions have completed architecturally and younger ones have not committed their effects. Implementation bookkeeping can restore that state after out-of-order execution.

Performing work before all conditions for its architectural execution are known, for example beyond a predicted branch. Invalid speculative results must not commit, but some cache or predictor effects can persist.

Processor storage holding pending stores and their addresses/data. A speculative store queue may track uncommitted stores; committed stores can also wait in a buffer before becoming externally visible, and suitable younger loads may receive forwarded data.

Supplying a load's value directly from an older store still waiting in the store buffer, when they access the same address, instead of waiting for the store to reach the cache. Real cores may require matching size and alignment.

Determining whether memory operations refer to conflicting locations so permitted loads and stores can overlap. A speculative implementation may let a load pass an older store with an unknown address, then detect a violation and recover.
Having several cache misses outstanding at once so their latencies overlap.

Very long instruction word: an ISA approach in which the compiler explicitly groups operations intended to run in parallel. Scheduling responsibilities, interlocks and support for variable latency depend on the particular architecture.

Explicitly parallel instruction computing, the design approach used by Intel Itanium, with compiler-visible operation groups, predication and speculation. It is related to VLIW but includes mechanisms addressing uncertain execution and latency.
Making an instruction's effect conditional on a predicate bit instead of branching around it.
The scheduler logic of an out-of-order core: compare each broadcast result tag with waiting operands (wakeup), then choose which ready instructions issue (select).

A numerical representation using a sign, significand and exponent, with format-specific exceptional values. A fixed-size floating-point format represents a finite collection of values, not every real number.

Power-delivery and heat-removal constraints on feasible processor operation. They contributed to increased emphasis on multicore and energy efficiency; they do not impose one universal clock-frequency ceiling.

Power associated with changing circuit state. Capacitive switching is commonly modelled using activity-weighted capacitance, supply voltage squared and switching frequency; total dynamic consumption can also include short-circuit effects.
Power that leaks through transistors even when they are not switching. It depends on voltage, temperature and transistor design.

A dimensionless measure of switching activity used with a stated power model. Here it is the capacitance-weighted mean charging events per cycle; the single-transition approximation uses zero to one and neglects additional intra-cycle glitches.
Electric charge stored per unit voltage, measured in farads. Charging and discharging circuit nodes consumes energy, which contributes to switching power.
The voltage powering a circuit, in volts. In a CMOS chip, dynamic power rises with its square, so lowering it saves a lot of power.

Complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor circuit technology using complementary transistor networks. Its power includes charging/discharging capacitances, short-circuit current during transitions and leakage; which contribution dominates depends on the implementation.
Metal-oxide-semiconductor field-effect transistor, the switch that CMOS chips are built from.

A transistor parameter describing the gate voltage associated with substantial channel conduction under specified conditions. The transition is not an ideal on/off boundary: subthreshold current remains, and threshold choices affect performance and leakage.

Ideal constant-field transistor scaling from Dennard and colleagues’ 1974 work: dimensions and voltage shrink together, allowing higher device speed at constant power per area under the model’s assumptions. Real processes do not indefinitely maintain all those scaling relationships.
example: With k = 0.7, power per transistor falls to 0.49 while transistors per area rise about 2.04 times.

definition: A historical projection of increasing component density in integrated circuits, later commonly expressed as roughly doubling transistor counts over about two years. It is an empirical trend and economic observation, not a physical law or a promise for every chip.
Power dissipated per unit area, for example watts per square millimetre. Local hot spots, cooling and package heat flow also matter; one average number does not determine temperature.
A processor containing multiple cores. It can improve concurrent-job throughput or accelerate parallel parts of one task; more cores alone do not divide a strictly serial thread’s execution time.

For a fixed job whose original execution-time fraction p scales perfectly over n equal workers, ideal speedup is the reciprocal of the serial fraction plus p divided by n. A nonzero serial fraction sets a finite ceiling; overhead and unequal workers need further modelling.
example: 90% parallel code on 8 cores gives about 4.7×, and never more than 10×.

definition: A scaled-workload view of parallel speedup: increasing the problem’s parallel work can make more processors useful even though the fixed-work serial-fraction model remains valid. Its conclusion requires a stated workload-scaling assumption.

Dynamic voltage and frequency scaling: choosing supported voltage/frequency operating points during execution. The permitted relationship and policy are platform-specific, and power savings do not alone determine total energy.
Running cores above their base frequency when power, current and thermal limits allow. Intel calls it Turbo Boost.

Finishing work quickly to permit lower-power idle operation afterwards. Whether it saves total energy compared with slower execution depends on voltage, static power, idle states and the whole system.
Suppressing selected clock transitions to reduce clock-related switching. Leakage remains, and changing data can still cause activity in ungated combinational paths.
Switching selected circuit supply domains off or into retention arrangements to reduce leakage. Entry/exit can cost time and energy, and other powered domains still consume power.

Cores with different performance or energy characteristics within one system. An energy-aware scheduler can choose a compatible placement meeting demand; a core labelled efficient is not guaranteed to use less total energy on every task.
A scheduler using workload demand and a model of CPU energy costs to choose suitable placements. Capacity, task affinity, system policy and overload behaviour also constrain the choice.
Chip area that cannot all run at full performance at the same time because of the power budget. Described in a 2011 study by Esmaeilzadeh and colleagues.

Hardware specialised for a class of operations, such as video encoding. It can improve throughput or energy efficiency for suitable work, but data movement, utilisation, programmability and implementation determine actual benefit.

A performance rate, such as completed jobs per second, divided by power in watts at a stated operating point. With matching intervals this is completed work per joule; workload definition and measurement scope matter.

Transforming operations so a vector or SIMD instruction handles multiple data elements. It can reduce dynamic instruction count, but supported operations, dependencies, vector length and extra setup affect the result.
Replicating a loop body several times per iteration to cut loop-control instructions, at the cost of bigger code.
The unit of frequency: one cycle per second.
10⁹ hertz: a billion cycles per second. A 3 GHz clock has a period of about 0.333 ns.
One billionth of a second, 10⁻⁹ s.
One trillionth of a second, 10⁻¹² s; 1,000 ps is 1 ns. This module's example pipeline stages take 100 to 300 ps.
The unit of power: one joule of energy per second.
The unit of voltage (electrical potential difference).
The unit of capacitance: one coulomb of charge per volt.
The power a base must be raised to to give a number: log₂(1,024) = 10.

GCC and Clang are open-source compiler implementations supporting C and C++ among other languages. They can optimise instruction selection, control flow and scheduling; their exact output depends on target, options and version.

The Arm instruction-set architecture family, including A32/T32 instructions in AArch32 and A64 instructions in AArch64. AArch64 uses 64-bit general-purpose registers, while A64 instructions themselves are 32-bit encodings.

Bits produced by instruction decode that tell later pipeline stages what to do, such as whether to read memory or write a register. They travel with the instruction through the pipeline registers; zeroing them turns a slot into a bubble.

The bounded collection of in-flight operations available for an out-of-order core to examine. Schedulers, the ROB, registers and memory queues impose different limits, so their capacities and instruction/micro-operation counts are not interchangeable.
A permitted power envelope for a chip, block or operating interval. Delivery, temperature, cooling, current and platform policy constrain it; temporary and sustained limits can differ.
In a load or store such as lw x1, 8(x2), the register (x2) whose value is added to the offset (8) to form the memory address.

The longest relevant propagation path between timing boundaries in a synchronous circuit. Together with storage and clock timing it limits the minimum clock period; it is not the project-management critical-path method.

An Intel performance-analysis method classifying pipeline-slot use into top-level categories such as retiring, bad speculation, front-end bound and back-end bound. It guides further investigation; categories concern slots and are not simply a sum of individual instruction latencies.

An exception for which the visible machine state does not correspond to the precise instruction boundary of the fault. Some older operations may be unfinished or younger results may already have taken effect.

The maximum amount of instruction decoding a stated front end can perform per cycle, measured in its specified instruction or micro-operation units. It can differ from issue, allocation and retirement width.

The maximum number of completed operations a core can commit per cycle under its counting convention. Dependencies, faults, blocked older work and implementation grouping can reduce the realised rate.

A teaching-model shorthand that must specify which stage and counting unit is four wide. When up to four architectural instructions complete per cycle, the corresponding ideal steady-state CPI is one quarter; real decode/issue/retirement widths can differ.

Reserving in-flight tracking resources such as ROB entries for incoming operations. An allocation rate says how many specified entries can be reserved per cycle; it does not guarantee ready instructions or retirement progress.

A classic MIPS branch form that nullifies its delay-slot instruction when the branch is not taken. This differs from normal delay-slot branches that execute the slot on either outcome, and availability depends on ISA revision.
Bits in an instruction encoding identifying a source or destination register. Keeping these fields in consistent positions can simplify decoding and register selection, as in the RISC-V base formats.
